detail:
In a 2024 Nature Communications paper, NIH researchers reported deep phenotyping of post-infectious ME/CFS: 17 participants who met rigorous criteria and 21 healthy controls underwent days of testing at the NIH Clinical Center, including brain imaging, exercise testing, immune profiling, and tissue sampling. The authors describe the pathophysiology as still unknown and note that no disease-modifying treatments are available.

One defining feature they report was an alteration of effort preference rather than physical or central fatigue, which they link to dysfunction of integrative brain regions and possible central catechol pathway dysregulation, with consequences for autonomic function and physical conditioning. Immune testing also found higher levels of naive B cells and lower levels of switched memory B cells in the ME/CFS group. The cohort was small, so the findings are directions for further study, not settled conclusions.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor before considering any research study.
sourceVideoTitle: Deep phenotyping of post-infectious myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
summary: A 2024 NIH study in Nature Communications intensively tested 17 people with post-infectious ME/CFS and 21 healthy controls, finding differences in effort preference, brain activity, and immune cell patterns that point research toward brain and immune mechanisms.
takeaways: the study used days of testing, from brain scans to muscle biopsies
findings point to brain regions involved in effort decisions
immune differences included naive and memory b cell shifts
it was a small study; results need replication, not self-treatment
title: Inside the NIH deep-phenotyping ME/CFS study
